newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - All-year suntans, yogic flying touted at election.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - All-year suntans, yogic flying touted at election.

text.p: The odds are 15 million-to-one against, but if Screaming Lord Sutch becomes the next prime minister Britons can hope for year-round suntans and decimal clocks.

Sutch's Monster Raving Loony Party says it would tow Britain 500 miles (800 km) south into the Atlantic to improve the climate in just one of a host of idealistic and outlandish manifesto pledges being made ahead of the May 1 election.
Its rival, the Rainbow Coalition, wants to rename Britain the "Emerald Rainbow Islands" and turn into a Utopia free of taxes and money and where all life's necessities come free.

The Natural Law Party promises to wipe out Britain's troubles by turning soldiers into yogic flyers. Convicted drug smuggler Howard Marks is standing for office as an independent on a pledge to legalise cannabis.
Fringe parties have long brightened Britain's political scene, dominated by the ruling Conservatives and Labour. Despite attempts to squeeze them out, fringe parties are on the rise.

In 1985, Britain introduced tighter conditions on anyone standing for parliament and raised the deposit they must pay to 500 pounds ($800) from 150 pounds. Candidates must win at least five percent of the vote or lose their deposit.
NUMBER OF FRINGE CANDIDATES ON THE RISE

Most fringe parties don't expect to get their money back but that doesn't seem to put them off. Since the early 1970s, the number of fringe candidates standing in British by-elections has risen from an average of three to more than seven.

There were around a dozen in the most recent parliamentary by-election in northwest England, including candidates for the 21st Century Independent Foresters, the Disillusioned Conservatives and an anti-smoking campaigner dressed as a smouldering cigarette.

The Monster Raving Loony Party plans to field at least 50 candidates in the election and Sutch himself will stand in several seats, among them the constituencies of Prime Minister John Major and opposition Labour leader Tony Blair.

Sutch, whose motto is "Vote for insanity, you know it makes sense", is Britain's longest-serving party leader. He has been standing in elections since 1963 and garnered more than 1,000 votes in one, his best result.

When Major stood on stage to hear the poll result in his constituency in the 1992 election, he was flanked on one side by Sutch wearing his trade-mark lurex suit and leopard-skin top hat and on the other by Lord Buckethead of the Gremloid Party, who claims to be a 267-year-old extraterrestrial visitor from the star system Alpha Centauri.
Lord Buckethead is yet to announce whether he will stand in May.
PARTY POLICIES

Sutch's latest policy proposals include plans to convert Britain's defunct coal mines into bungee-jumping centres -- making local politicians the first to test them -- and to make all dogs eat phosphorescent food so that no-one need fear treading in dog mess at night.
He would introduce decimal time with 10-hour days and 10-minute hours. "Current time-keeping is too confusing, especially when you're hungover and late for work," says the Loonies' manifesto.
The Loony Party's biggest rival for votes is likely to be the Rainbow Coalition, whose campaign so far has been carried out by recorded telephone message.

Against a backdrop of soaring synthesizer music, a woman's spacey voice welcomes callers to "five minutes that will change your life". She goes on to set out the party's democratic vision, which centres around endless referenda conducted on the Internet.

Standing a slightly better chance of winning votes is the Natural Law Party, formed in 1992 by followers of Maharashi Mahesh Yogi -- the Indian mystic who converted the Beatles to transcendental meditation in the 1960s.

The Natural Law Party intends to recruit 7,000 yogic flyers from the ranks of the armed forces to create a "prevention wing" whose efforts would eliminate Britain's "collective stress", bringing about peace, harmony and lower taxes.

"The prevention wing would eliminate conflict at its source by preventing the birth of an enemy," says the Natural Law Party, which won 0.4 percent of the vote in the 1992 election and plans to field 350 candidates in May.
Howard Marks hands out cannabis snacks at news conferences to publicise his one-man campaign.

Other electoral no-hopers include Paul Kay of the British Anarchist Party, whose lengthy but vague manifesto promises to make alcohol and tobacco prices "the same as abroad" and pledges half-price holidays for the poor and unemployed.

And just to ensure that Britons get it right when they enter the polling booths next month, white witch Kevin Carlyon has been casting spells at Downing Street, the official home of Britain's prime ministers.
"Kevin has no personal interest in the government, but he does feel a responsibility in helping both his followers and members of the public," his pagan church said in a statement.
